question: to the Commission Jadwiga Wiśniewska (ECR) Subject:

The EU has banned a number of active substances in agriculture, such as thiophanate-methyl, carbendazim and benomyl, because of their potentially harmful effects on human health and the environment. At the same time, agricultural products imported from third countries – including fruit and vegetables such as mangoes, papayas, citrus fruits and grapes, as well as other plant products – that may contain residues of these substances continue to enter the EU market. This situation raises serious doubts as to the coherence of EU regulations and the equal treatment of producers. Farmers in the EU are required to comply with strict standards and bear the associated costs, while products produced using substances banned in the EU can compete with them in the single market. In this connection: How does the Commission assess the impact of the current rules allowing imports of products containing residues of substances not authorised in the EU on the competitiveness of EU agricultural producers? The current legal situation undermines the credibility of the EU’s food safety policy, the protection of citizens’ health and the coherence of single market rules.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.8.2026) Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 on maximum residues levels (MRLs) of pesticides1 ensures the safety of food and feed products, for both domestically and imported products, through a rigorous, science-based risk assessment process. The Regulation allows setting MRLs for imported agricultural products that contain residues of active substances, but only if these MRLs are safe for EU consumers. This possibility contributes to food and feed security – in particular for commodities for which the EU is not self-sufficient – while ensuring that imported food meets the EU’s high safety standards. As regards the specific substances referred to by the Honourable Member, the Commission has adopted a Regulation on 8 July 2026 to lower all MRLs for carbendazim, benomyl and thiophanate-methyl to the technical zero2. More generally, in the Vision for Agriculture and Food3, the Commission announced that it will establish a principle that the most hazardous pesticides banned in the EU for health and environmental reasons are not allowed back to the EU through imported products. To advance on this, the Commission has launched a study4 that will inform an impact assessment that will consider the impacts on the EU’s competitive position and the international implications and, if appropriate, amendments to the applicable legal framework will be proposed. The Commission has also proposed in the Food and Feed Safety Simplification Package5 to establish the possibility to lower MRLs to the technical zero for the most hazardous substances6 not approved in the EU on a case-by-case basis, if considered appropriate, in the light of the outcome of substance-specific assessments.

f. 5 https://food.ec.europa.eu/horizontal-topics/simplification-legislation_en. 6 Substances having one or more of the following characteristics: Mutagen Cat. 1A or 1B; Carcinogen Cat. 1A or 1B; Toxic for reproduction Cat. 1A or 1B; Persistent organic pollutants (POP); Persistent, bioaccumulative and toxic (PBT) substances; very persistent and very bioaccumulative (vPvB) substances; as well as Endocrine disruptors for human health and/or for non- target organisms.
